title: Steam or smoke from under the hood
h1: Why is steam or smoke coming from under my hood?
metaDesc: Steam or smoke from under the hood? Answer a few quick questions to see if it's overheating, a coolant or oil leak, or just water, and how urgent it is.
synonyms: smoke from hood but not overheating
smoke under the hood wont stop
intro: Steam can come from the cooling system; smoke can signal a fire. They can be hard to tell apart. Use what you already noticed from safety. The questions cover warning lights, recent conditions and next steps.
safety: If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
Never open the radiator cap or coolant tank cap on a hot engine. The coolant is under pressure and can spray out and burn you.
If the temperature gauge is in the red, pull over and turn off the engine as soon as it's safe.
Keep the hood closed while steam or spray is escaping. If you cannot tell steam from smoke, stay away and call 911 if a fire is possible.

q_danger.q: Do you suspect a fire, or is the engine overheating?
q_danger.help: The temperature gauge usually has a C (cold) and H (hot) or a thermometer symbol. Some cars only have a red or blue thermometer warning light instead of a gauge.

opts.a: I see flames, smoke with a burning smell, or other signs of a possible fire
The temperature gauge is in the red, or a red temperature warning light is on
Neither of these: the gauge looks normal

q_smell.q: What odor did you notice before you moved away?
q_smell.help: Stay away from escaping vapor or smoke. Choose “I'm not sure” if you did not notice an odor.

opts.a: Sweet, a bit like syrup or maple
No real smell, just light white wisps

q_coolant.q: What did you already notice from a safe distance?
q_coolant.help: Keep the hood closed while steam or coolant is escaping. You can choose “I'm not sure.”

opts.a: Coolant spraying or pouring out, or a big puddle forming fast
Coolant bubbling or boiling out of the overflow tank
A slow drip, or a wet or crusty spot on a hose or the radiator
I can't see where it's coming from / I'm not sure
After rain, a car wash, or driving through puddles or snow, and it faded within a few minutes
Within a few days after an oil change or other engine work
It's actually from the tailpipe on a cold morning, not the hood
It keeps coming every time I drive, even in dry weather

result.title: This could be an engine fire starting. Get away from the car
result.now: Pull over safely, turn off the vehicle and get everyone out. Smoke with a burning smell can mean a fire even without visible flames. Stay at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911. Leave the hood closed and do not return to the vehicle.
if: Even if the smoke stops, stay away until responders say it is safe. Arrange a tow before using the vehicle again.
result.why: Flames or thick, darkening smoke mean something is burning, not just steam. Opening the hood lets in a rush of air that can make a fire flare up suddenly, and fuel lines and tires can burn quickly.

causes.name: Fuel leaking onto hot engine or exhaust parts
causes.clues: A strong gasoline smell before or with the smoke.

causes.name: Electrical short or melting wiring
causes.clues: A burning plastic smell, fuses blowing, or lights and gauges acting up beforehand.

causes.name: Oil or other fluid burning on the exhaust
causes.clues: A recent oil leak or engine work, and a heavy burning oil smell.

result.title: The engine is overheating. Stop now to avoid serious damage
result.now: Pull over safely and switch the engine off. Keep the hood closed while steam or spray is escaping. Leave all coolant caps in place until the engine and radiator are fully cold. Arrange roadside help or a tow before restarting.
if: If you're in a dangerous spot and need a moment to reach a safe place, turn the heater to full hot with the fan on high. It pulls some heat away from the engine.
If the coolant tank is empty once the engine is cool, there's a leak or another fault behind it. Topping it up doesn't fix the cause, so still have it checked before relying on the car.
If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
result.why: Steam with the gauge in the red means the engine is running far hotter than it's designed to. Keeping it running can warp the cylinder head or blow the head gasket, turning a simple repair into a major one.

causes.name: Coolant leak (hose, radiator or water pump)
causes.clues: A sweet smell, coolant under the car, or a low overflow tank.

causes.name: Radiator fan not working
causes.clues: It overheated in traffic or at idle but was fine on the highway.
causes.against: If it overheated at highway speed, the fan is a less likely cause.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck closed
causes.clues: The gauge climbed quickly after a normal start, with no visible leak.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Coolant keeps disappearing with no leak, white smoke from the tailpipe, or bubbles in the coolant tank.

result.title: A coolant hose, the radiator or the water pump may be leaking badly
result.now: Pull over safely and switch the engine off. Keep the hood closed while steam or spray is escaping. Leave all coolant caps in place until the engine and radiator are fully cold. Arrange roadside help or a tow before restarting.
if: If the temperature gauge was already climbing before you stopped, mention it to the shop so they check for heat damage too.
If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
result.why: When coolant is pouring out, the engine will lose most of it within minutes and overheat quickly. Running it even a short distance this way can cause serious engine damage.

causes.name: Burst or split coolant hose
causes.clues: Coolant spraying from a rubber hose near the top or front of the engine.

causes.name: Cracked radiator or radiator seam
causes.clues: Coolant pouring from behind the front grille.

causes.name: Failed water pump
causes.clues: Coolant pouring from the front of the engine, near the drive belt.

shop: Visual inspection of hoses, radiator and water pump

result.title: Coolant boiling over usually means the engine is overheating
result.now: Pull over safely and switch the engine off. Keep the hood closed while steam or spray is escaping. Leave all coolant caps in place until the engine and radiator are fully cold. Arrange roadside help or a tow before restarting.
if: If the gauge reads normal, don't trust it. When coolant is low, the sensor can read low even though the engine is very hot.
If you see bubbles in the tank with the engine running and fully warm, tell the shop. That can be a sign of a head gasket leak.
result.why: Coolant boiling out of the overflow tank means it's getting hotter than the system can handle. That happens when coolant is low, flow is blocked, the cap isn't holding pressure, or exhaust gases are leaking into the coolant.

causes.name: Low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, drips under the car, or the tank has been low before.

causes.name: Faulty radiator or tank cap
causes.clues: Coolant seeps from around the cap, but there's no other leak.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck or fan not working
causes.clues: It happened in traffic or soon after a normal start.

causes.name: Head gasket leak
causes.clues: Coolant keeps disappearing, white smoke from the tailpipe, or constant bubbling in the tank.

result.title: Coolant may be leaking onto hot engine parts
result.now: Pull over safely and switch the engine off. Keep the hood closed while steam or spray is escaping. Leave all coolant caps in place until the engine and radiator are fully cold. Arrange roadside help or a tow before restarting.
if: If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
Tell roadside assistance about any puddle, steam or coolant loss you already saw.
result.why: A sweet smell or steam with a normal temperature gauge often comes from a small amount of coolant dripping or seeping onto hot parts and steaming off. Leaks tend to grow, and running low on coolant will make the engine overheat. When coolant is very low, the gauge can also read normal even though the engine is hot, so the level check matters more than the gauge.

causes.name: Leaking hose or loose hose clamp
causes.clues: A wet or crusty spot where a rubber hose connects.

causes.name: Leaking radiator
causes.clues: Drips or crusty colored residue at the front of the car.

causes.name: Water pump seal leak
causes.clues: Drips or residue near the drive belt at the front of the engine.

causes.name: Heater core leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside the car, foggy windows, or a damp passenger-side floor.
causes.against: Steam from under the hood alone points more to the engine bay than the heater core.

you: Check the coolant level through the marked reservoir only when the engine is fully cold.

result.title: Oil may be dripping onto the hot exhaust
result.now: Pull over safely, switch the engine off and move everyone away. If there is smoke with a burning smell, follow the fire warning and call 911 from at least 100 feet away. If the smoke has already stopped, keep the engine off and arrange a tow or inspection where it is.
if: If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
Even if the smoke stops, stay away until responders say it is safe. Arrange a tow before using the vehicle again.
result.why: Oil smoking on the exhaust gives off a heavy, sharp burning smell and bluish-white smoke. Common causes are a leaking gasket or a loose part, but oil on hot parts is a fire risk and the engine can run low on oil.

causes.name: Leaking valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oily residue along the top edge of the engine.

causes.name: Spill or loose part from a recent oil change
causes.clues: It started right after a service, and the oil filter or filler cap area is wet.

causes.name: Other engine oil leak
causes.clues: Brown or black drops under the car.

shop: Oil leak inspection (sometimes with UV dye)
Oil filter and drain plug check

result.title: Something may be melting or a belt may be burning. Don't keep running it
result.now: Pull over safely, turn off the vehicle and get everyone out. Smoke with a burning smell can mean a fire even without visible flames. Stay at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911. Leave the hood closed and do not return to the vehicle.
if: Even if the smoke stops, stay away until responders say it is safe. Arrange a tow before using the vehicle again.
result.why: Burning rubber or plastic smells mean something that shouldn't be getting hot is. A belt slipping on a seized pulley, melting wiring, or debris on the exhaust can each start a fire if you keep going.

causes.name: Drive belt slipping on a seized pulley or A/C compressor
causes.clues: A squeal before the smell, or the smell is strongest at the front of the engine.

causes.name: Electrical short or melting wiring
causes.clues: A sharp plastic smell, blown fuses, or electrical items acting up.

causes.name: Plastic bag or road debris on the exhaust
causes.clues: It started right after driving over something.

result.title: This could be water steaming off hot engine parts
result.now: Watch it for a few minutes. If the steam fades, has no smell and the temperature gauge stays in its normal spot, water burning off is the likely explanation. Check the coolant level the next time the engine is cold.
if: If vapor returns in dry weather, park safely and switch off. Have the cooling system checked before driving again.
If you notice a sweet smell, or the coolant level is below MIN, treat it as a coolant leak and get it checked.
If the gauge climbs toward the red or a temperature warning light comes on, pull over and turn off the engine.
If you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911 from there. Leave the hood closed and stay away.
result.why: Rain, a car wash or splashing through puddles leaves water on the hot engine and exhaust. It turns to light, odorless white steam that disappears quickly. That's common and usually stops on its own once things dry out.

causes.name: Rain or wash water evaporating
causes.clues: It happened after wet weather or washing, faded quickly, and had no smell.
causes.against: A sweet or burning smell points to something else.

causes.name: Small coolant seep
causes.clues: It keeps happening in dry weather, or the coolant tank drops over time.

you: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold.
shop: Cooling system pressure test if the steam keeps coming back

result.title: White vapor from the tailpipe on a cold morning is usually normal
result.now: Watch whether the vapor fades once the engine is fully warmed up, usually within 10 to 15 minutes of driving.
if: If thick white smoke continues after the engine is warm, especially with a sweet smell, get it checked before relying on the car. Coolant may be leaking inside the engine.
If the coolant level keeps dropping with no leak you can find, ask the shop to test for a head gasket leak.
If the temperature gauge climbs toward the red or a temperature warning light comes on, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: Burning fuel makes water vapor. When the engine and exhaust are cold, that vapor condenses into white clouds out of the tailpipe. Once things warm up, it should become hard to see.

causes.name: Normal condensation
causes.clues: Cold or damp weather, thin vapor that fades as the engine warms, no smell.
causes.against: Thick smoke that keeps going after warm-up is not normal.

causes.name: Coolant burning inside the engine (head gasket)
causes.clues: Thick white smoke after warm-up, a sweet smell, and a coolant level that keeps dropping.

you: Note whether the vapor stops once the car is fully warm.
Check the coolant level once a week for a few weeks.

result.title: Treat it as overheating until you know it isn't
result.now: Pull over safely and switch the engine off. Keep the hood closed. If smoke or a burning odor makes you suspect a fire, get everyone at least 100 feet away, clear of traffic, and call 911. If it is steam, stay back until it clears and arrange roadside help before restarting.
if: If you called the fire department, wait away from the vehicle until responders say it is safe.
result.why: Without knowing the temperature reading or the smell, it's hard to rule out overheating, and driving an overheating engine can ruin it quickly. Stopping costs a few minutes; guessing wrong can cost the engine.

causes.name: Engine overheating
causes.clues: The gauge climbs, the heater blows cold, or there's a sweet smell.

causes.name: Coolant or oil leaking onto hot parts
causes.clues: A sweet or burning oil smell.

causes.name: Water evaporating
causes.clues: Recent rain or a car wash, and it faded quickly with no smell.
